claims.text: Large clustered keys can increase both collection storage and secondary-index storage. Secondary indexes refer to the clustered key's encoded RecordId, so clustering can trade the removed _id index against larger secondary-index references. (high confidence)

Clustering removes one separately maintained _id structure, but that alone does not establish a throughput gain. Percona explicitly cautions that clustered writes may be slower, while MongoDB documents potential insert benefits and a random-key penalty; neither statement is a universal benchmark result. (medium confidence)

The statement that MongoDB cannot store index-organized collections is obsolete as a blanket claim: the critical article itself adds a footnote acknowledging clustered collections beginning with MongoDB 5.3. Its ordinary-collection discussion should not be applied to explicitly clustered collections. (high confidence)

The current manual requires a clustered index on { _id: 1 } and creation of that index when the collection is created. An existing ordinary collection cannot be converted in place; documents must be copied into another collection. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)

Cache capacity scopes the random-insert penalty. MongoDB describes eviction and replacement when random index entries no longer fit cache; combined with the clustered-document locality mechanism, this supports testing cache-resident and larger-than-cache workloads separately, rather than assigning a fixed UUID slowdown. This testing recommendation is an inference, not a measured clustered-collection result. (medium confidence)

MongoDB clustered collections store documents in _id key order in one WiredTiger file, eliminating the separate default _id index. This makes application key order determine document placement. (high confidence)

With random UUIDv4 _id values, inserts into a clustered collection scatter document writes across the tree and reduce cache locality. Increasing keys concentrate insert activity; MongoDB recommends sequentially increasing clustered keys and warns that random keys may reduce performance. (high confidence)

For ordinary non-clustered collections, random _id values scatter the _id index entries without making document placement follow _id order. The document tree instead uses internal RecordIds; clustered collections derive an order-preserving RecordId from _id. (medium confidence)

Clustering eliminates the separate _id index: an _id lookup reaches the document through one tree traversal, and inserts avoid maintaining a second tree for that index. This describes logical tree work, not a guarantee of one physical disk I/O or the absence of journal and secondary-index writes. (high confidence)
